children.proof_nl:
Fix an arbitrary positive integer d. Define
A := {i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}
and
B := {i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}.

We split the index set {1,...,b} into the disjoint union {1,...,a} union {a+1,...,b}. (If a=0 or a=b, one of these sets is empty, and the same argument still applies.) Therefore A is the disjoint union of A ∩ {1,...,a} and A ∩ {a+1,...,b}, and similarly for B.

For i with 1 <= i <= a, the definition gives e_i = i. Hence
|A ∩ {1,...,a}| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}|.

For i with a < i <= b, the definition gives e_i = r+i. The map i -> r+i is a bijection from {a+1,...,b} onto the set {m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b}. Under this bijection, the condition d divides e_i is exactly the condition d divides m. Thus
|A ∩ {a+1,...,b}| = |{m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b and d divides m}| = M_d(r+a,r+b).

Since the two pieces are disjoint,
|A| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}| + M_d(r+a,r+b).

Now do the same for B. Clearly,
|B ∩ {1,...,a}| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}|.
Also, the identity map is a bijection from {a+1,...,b} onto {m in Z : a < m <= b}, so
|B ∩ {a+1,...,b}| = |{m in Z : a < m <= b and d divides m}| = M_d(a,b).
Therefore,
|B| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}| + M_d(a,b).

By the hypothesis of the lemma, for this positive integer d we have
M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b).
Comparing the formulas for |A| and |B|, we obtain
|A| >= |B|,
that is,
|{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|.

Because d was arbitrary, this holds for every positive integer d, exactly as claimed.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every choice of integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, if every positive integer d has at least as many multiples in the interval from r + a to r + b as in the interval from a to b, then for every positive integer d the number of indices i from 1 through b for which d divides e_i is at least the number of indices i from 1 through b for which d divides i.
quantifier_order: Fix integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0.
For each integer i with 1 <= i <= b, define e_i by a piecewise rule: e_i = i if i <= a, and e_i = r + i if a < i <= b.
For each positive integer d and integers u, v, define M_d(u, v) as the number of integers m satisfying u < m <= v and d divides m.
Assume that for every positive integer d, M_d(r + a, r + b) is at least M_d(a, b).
Conclude that for every positive integer d, the number of indices i from 1 through b with d dividing e_i is at least the number of indices i from 1 through b with d dividing i.

children.statement_nl: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. For 1 <= i <= b define an integer e_i by e_i = i when i <= a, and e_i = r+i when a < i <= b. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. If M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d, then for every positive integer d one has |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|.

status_snapshot.last_transition_reason: The proof is a complete direct counting argument. For fixed positive d, it partitions the index set {1,...,b} into {1,...,a} and {a+1,...,b}, uses the definition e_i=i on the first part and e_i=r+i on the second, and identifies the second-part count with M_d(r+a,r+b). Doing the same for divisibility of i identifies the comparison count with M_d(a,b). The assumed inequality then gives the desired result. The proof matches the lemma statement and assembly role, and it uses no undeclared or forbidden dependencies.

children.statement_nl: Let b be a nonnegative integer, and let e_1,...,e_b be an ordered list of b positive integers. Let S := Q[y_1,...,y_b] be the polynomial ring graded by deg(y_i)=i for 1 <= i <= b. Assume that for every positive integer d, one has |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials u_1,...,u_b in S such that deg(u_i)=e_i for every i and the ordered list u_1,...,u_b is a regular sequence. When b=0, this means the empty regular sequence in S=Q.

status_snapshot.last_transition_reason: The submitted proof is empty, and the lemma statement is refuted by the supplied counterexample. For b=3 and (e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,1,6), the divisibility hypothesis holds for every positive integer d: for d=1,2,3 both sides are equal, and for d>=4 the right-hand side is 0. But in S=Q[y_1,y_2,y_3] with weighted degrees deg(y_i)=i, the homogeneous degree-1 subspace is one-dimensional, spanned by y_1. Hence any homogeneous u_1,u_2 of degree 1 are proportional. If u_1=0 then the sequence is not regular; if u_1!=0 then u_2 lies in (u_1), so its image in S/(u_1) is 0, which is not a non-zero-divisor in the nonzero ring S/(u_1). Therefore no regular sequence u_1,u_2,u_3 with degrees 1,1,6 exists.

Suppose g_1,...,g_a are homogeneous elements of S that form a regular sequence and satisfy deg(g_i)=i for each i=1,...,a. Then there exists a graded Q-algebra automorphism phi : S -> S such that phi(g_i)=y_i for every i=1,...,a. When a=0, phi may be taken to be the identity automorphism.

children.proof_nl: Let v_i := phi(u_i) for i = 1,...,n. For each i = 0,...,n, set I_i := (u_1,...,u_i) and J_i := (v_1,...,v_i), with I_0 = J_0 = (0). Because phi is an algebra automorphism, phi(I_i) = J_i for every i. Hence phi induces an isomorphism of quotient rings bar_phi_i : A / I_i -> A / J_i, given by a + I_i |-> phi(a) + J_i; its inverse is induced by phi^{-1}. Now let u_i have degree d. Since phi is a graded automorphism, it preserves each graded piece, so phi(u_i) also lies in the degree-d piece. Therefore deg(phi(u_i)) = d = deg(u_i) for every i. It remains to prove preservation of regular sequences. Use the standard ring-theoretic definition: a sequence x_1,...,x_n is regular if for each i >= 1, the class of x_i is a non-zero-divisor in A / (x_1,...,x_{i-1}); if one also adopts the common extra condition that the final quotient A / (x_1,...,x_n) be nonzero, that condition is also preserved here because the final quotients are isomorphic. Assume first that u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence. Fix i with 1 <= i <= n. Suppose that in A / J_{i-1} one has (v_i + J_{i-1})(a + J_{i-1}) = 0. Then v_i a is in J_{i-1} = phi(I_{i-1}). Applying phi^{-1}, we get u_i phi^{-1}(a) in I_{i-1}. Equivalently, in A / I_{i-1} we have (u_i + I_{i-1})(phi^{-1}(a) + I_{i-1}) = 0. Since u_i + I_{i-1} is a non-zero-divisor in A / I_{i-1}, it follows that phi^{-1}(a) + I_{i-1} = 0, so phi^{-1}(a) is in I_{i-1}. Applying phi, we obtain a in J_{i-1}. Thus v_i + J_{i-1} is a non-zero-divisor in A / J_{i-1}. Since this holds for every i, the sequence v_1,...,v_n is regular. If one includes the additional condition A / I_n != 0 in the definition, it is preserved as well because bar_phi_n is an isomorphism A / I_n ~= A / J_n. Conversely, if v_1,...,v_n is regular, the same argument applied to the automorphism phi^{-1} shows that u_1,...,u_n is regular. Therefore u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence if and only if phi(u_1),...,phi(u_n) is a regular sequence. Together with the degree argument above, this proves the lemma.

children.proof_nl:
Let I = (u_1,...,u_m) and B = A/I, and for each j let w_j be the image of v_j in B. For each integer t with 0 <= t <= n, set J_t = (u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_t) in A, with J_0 = I. Because the concatenated sequence u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_n is regular in A, two facts hold: each J_t is a proper ideal of A, and for each j with 1 <= j <= n, the element v_j is a nonzerodivisor on A/J_{j-1}.

First we prove the proper-ideal condition in B. Fix t with 0 <= t <= n. Suppose that the ideal (w_1,...,w_t) is all of B. Then there are elements b_1,...,b_t in B such that 1 = sum b_i w_i in B; when t = 0 this just means 1 = 0 in B. Choose lifts a_i in A of the elements b_i. Then 1 - sum a_i v_i lies in I, so 1 lies in I + (v_1,...,v_t) = J_t. This contradicts the fact that J_t is proper. Hence (w_1,...,w_t) is a proper ideal of B for every t. In particular, taking t = 0 shows that B is not the zero ring.

Next we prove the nonzerodivisor condition. Fix j with 1 <= j <= n. Let x be an element of A whose class in B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is annihilated by w_j. By definition of the quotient, this means that v_j x lies in I + (v_1,...,v_{j-1}) = J_{j-1}. Since v_j is a nonzerodivisor on A/J_{j-1}, it follows that x lies in J_{j-1}. But then the class of x in B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is zero. Therefore multiplication by w_j on B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is injective, so w_j is a nonzerodivisor there.

Thus every initial ideal (w_1,...,w_t) is proper in B, and each w_j is a nonzerodivisor modulo the preceding ones. Hence w_1,...,w_n is a regular sequence in B = A/(u_1,...,u_m).

Now assume A is graded and all u_i and v_j are homogeneous. Then I = (u_1,...,u_m) is a homogeneous ideal, so B = A/I inherits the quotient grading, and the quotient map A -> B preserves degrees. Therefore the image w_j of a homogeneous element v_j of degree d lies in the degree-d part of B. Since w_j is nonzero by the regularity already proved, this means that w_j is homogeneous of degree d, so it has the same degree as v_j. This proves the graded statement as well.

decomposition.assembled_proof_nl:
Target: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}, and let R := Q[x_s : s in I] be the polynomial ring graded by deg(x_s) = s for each s in I. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. Assume M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Then there exists a family (f_s)_{s in I} of homogeneous polynomials in R such that deg(f_s) = r+s for every s in I, and the ordered list of these polynomials in increasing order of s is a regular sequence in R. If I is empty, this means the empty family.

Strategy summary: Embed the target ring R = Q[x_s : s in {a+1,...,b}] into the larger weighted polynomial ring S = Q[y_1,...,y_b] by viewing R as the quotient S/(y_1,...,y_a). Package the desired tail degrees together with the killed coordinate degrees into the ordered list (1,2,...,a,r+a+1,...,r+b). The given interval divisibility hypothesis is exactly the divisor-count dominance needed for a stronger existence theorem in the initial-interval ring S. After obtaining a regular sequence in S of those degrees, straighten the first a entries to y_1,...,y_a by a graded triangular automorphism, then descend the remaining entries to the quotient ring R.

Assembly skeleton: Work in the larger weighted polynomial ring S = Q[y_1,...,y_b] with weights 1,...,b, and encode the desired construction by the ordered degree list e_i = i for i <= a and e_i = r+i for i > a. The theorem hypothesis is exactly the divisor-count condition for this list, so the bottleneck initial-interval existence theorem yields a homogeneous regular sequence u_1,...,u_b in S with those ordered degrees. The first a elements have degrees 1,...,a, so a graded triangular automorphism straightens them to the coordinate variables y_1,...,y_a. Quotienting by those variables leaves the tail as a regular sequence in S/(y_1,...,y_a), and this quotient is canonically the target ring R = Q[x_s : s in {a+1,...,b}]. The descended tail gives the family (f_s)_{s in I} with deg(f_s)=r+s in increasing order. If a=b, the tail is empty, so the witness family is the empty family.

1. lem_20260329132335_f096b04e: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. For 1 <= i <= b define an integer e_i by e_i = i when i <= a, and e_i = r+i when a < i <= b. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. If M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d, then for every positive integer d one has |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|.
Fix an arbitrary positive integer d. Define
A := {i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}
and
B := {i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}.

We split the index set {1,...,b} into the disjoint union {1,...,a} union {a+1,...,b}. (If a=0 or a=b, one of these sets is empty, and the same argument still applies.) Therefore A is the disjoint union of A ∩ {1,...,a} and A ∩ {a+1,...,b}, and similarly for B.

For i with 1 <= i <= a, the definition gives e_i = i. Hence
|A ∩ {1,...,a}| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}|.

For i with a < i <= b, the definition gives e_i = r+i. The map i -> r+i is a bijection from {a+1,...,b} onto the set {m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b}. Under this bijection, the condition d divides e_i is exactly the condition d divides m. Thus
|A ∩ {a+1,...,b}| = |{m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b and d divides m}| = M_d(r+a,r+b).

Since the two pieces are disjoint,
|A| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}| + M_d(r+a,r+b).

Now do the same for B. Clearly,
|B ∩ {1,...,a}| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}|.
Also, the identity map is a bijection from {a+1,...,b} onto {m in Z : a < m <= b}, so
|B ∩ {a+1,...,b}| = |{m in Z : a < m <= b and d divides m}| = M_d(a,b).
Therefore,
|B| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}| + M_d(a,b).

By the hypothesis of the lemma, for this positive integer d we have
M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b).
Comparing the formulas for |A| and |B|, we obtain
|A| >= |B|,
that is,
|{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|.

Because d was arbitrary, this holds for every positive integer d, exactly as claimed.

4. lem_20260329132425_b7fb9eda: Let A be a graded commutative Q-algebra, let phi : A -> A be a graded Q-algebra automorphism, and let u_1,...,u_n be homogeneous elements of A. Then u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence if and only if phi(u_1),...,phi(u_n) is a regular sequence. Moreover deg(phi(u_i)) = deg(u_i) for every i.
Let v_i := phi(u_i) for i = 1,...,n. For each i = 0,...,n, set I_i := (u_1,...,u_i) and J_i := (v_1,...,v_i), with I_0 = J_0 = (0). Because phi is an algebra automorphism, phi(I_i) = J_i for every i. Hence phi induces an isomorphism of quotient rings bar_phi_i : A / I_i -> A / J_i, given by a + I_i |-> phi(a) + J_i; its inverse is induced by phi^{-1}. Now let u_i have degree d. Since phi is a graded automorphism, it preserves each graded piece, so phi(u_i) also lies in the degree-d piece. Therefore deg(phi(u_i)) = d = deg(u_i) for every i. It remains to prove preservation of regular sequences. Use the standard ring-theoretic definition: a sequence x_1,...,x_n is regular if for each i >= 1, the class of x_i is a non-zero-divisor in A / (x_1,...,x_{i-1}); if one also adopts the common extra condition that the final quotient A / (x_1,...,x_n) be nonzero, that condition is also preserved here because the final quotients are isomorphic. Assume first that u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence. Fix i with 1 <= i <= n. Suppose that in A / J_{i-1} one has (v_i + J_{i-1})(a + J_{i-1}) = 0. Then v_i a is in J_{i-1} = phi(I_{i-1}). Applying phi^{-1}, we get u_i phi^{-1}(a) in I_{i-1}. Equivalently, in A / I_{i-1} we have (u_i + I_{i-1})(phi^{-1}(a) + I_{i-1}) = 0. Since u_i + I_{i-1} is a non-zero-divisor in A / I_{i-1}, it follows that phi^{-1}(a) + I_{i-1} = 0, so phi^{-1}(a) is in I_{i-1}. Applying phi, we obtain a in J_{i-1}. Thus v_i + J_{i-1} is a non-zero-divisor in A / J_{i-1}. Since this holds for every i, the sequence v_1,...,v_n is regular. If one includes the additional condition A / I_n != 0 in the definition, it is preserved as well because bar_phi_n is an isomorphism A / I_n ~= A / J_n. Conversely, if v_1,...,v_n is regular, the same argument applied to the automorphism phi^{-1} shows that u_1,...,u_n is regular. Therefore u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence if and only if phi(u_1),...,phi(u_n) is a regular sequence. Together with the degree argument above, this proves the lemma.

5. lem_20260329132438_1d671bdc: Let A be a commutative ring, and let u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_n be a regular sequence in A. Then the images of v_1,...,v_n in the quotient ring A/(u_1,...,u_m) form a regular sequence. If A is graded and all u_i and v_j are homogeneous, then the quotient images are homogeneous and keep the same degrees.
Let I = (u_1,...,u_m) and B = A/I, and for each j let w_j be the image of v_j in B. For each integer t with 0 <= t <= n, set J_t = (u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_t) in A, with J_0 = I. Because the concatenated sequence u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_n is regular in A, two facts hold: each J_t is a proper ideal of A, and for each j with 1 <= j <= n, the element v_j is a nonzerodivisor on A/J_{j-1}.

First we prove the proper-ideal condition in B. Fix t with 0 <= t <= n. Suppose that the ideal (w_1,...,w_t) is all of B. Then there are elements b_1,...,b_t in B such that 1 = sum b_i w_i in B; when t = 0 this just means 1 = 0 in B. Choose lifts a_i in A of the elements b_i. Then 1 - sum a_i v_i lies in I, so 1 lies in I + (v_1,...,v_t) = J_t. This contradicts the fact that J_t is proper. Hence (w_1,...,w_t) is a proper ideal of B for every t. In particular, taking t = 0 shows that B is not the zero ring.

Next we prove the nonzerodivisor condition. Fix j with 1 <= j <= n. Let x be an element of A whose class in B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is annihilated by w_j. By definition of the quotient, this means that v_j x lies in I + (v_1,...,v_{j-1}) = J_{j-1}. Since v_j is a nonzerodivisor on A/J_{j-1}, it follows that x lies in J_{j-1}. But then the class of x in B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is zero. Therefore multiplication by w_j on B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is injective, so w_j is a nonzerodivisor there.

Thus every initial ideal (w_1,...,w_t) is proper in B, and each w_j is a nonzerodivisor modulo the preceding ones. Hence w_1,...,w_n is a regular sequence in B = A/(u_1,...,u_m).

Now assume A is graded and all u_i and v_j are homogeneous. Then I = (u_1,...,u_m) is a homogeneous ideal, so B = A/I inherits the quotient grading, and the quotient map A -> B preserves degrees. Therefore the image w_j of a homogeneous element v_j of degree d lies in the degree-d part of B. Since w_j is nonzero by the regularity already proved, this means that w_j is homogeneous of degree d, so it has the same degree as v_j. This proves the graded statement as well.

6. lem_20260329132447_75e7cd4d: Let a and b be integers with 0 <= a <= b. Put I := {a+1,...,b}, let S := Q[y_1,...,y_b] with weighted grading deg(y_i)=i, and let R := Q[x_s : s in I] with weighted grading deg(x_s)=s. Then the quotient S/(y_1,...,y_a) is canonically isomorphic to R as a graded Q-algebra, via the map sending the class of y_s to x_s for each s in I. Under this graded isomorphism, homogeneous regular sequences correspond and weighted degrees are preserved. When a=b, both rings are Q.

4. lem_20260329132425_b7fb9eda: Let A be a graded commutative Q-algebra, let phi : A -> A be a graded Q-algebra automorphism, and let u_1,...,u_n be homogeneous elements of A. Then u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence if and only if phi(u_1),...,phi(u_n) is a regular sequence. Moreover deg(phi(u_i)) = deg(u_i) for every i.
Let v_i := phi(u_i) for i = 1,...,n. For each i = 0,...,n, set I_i := (u_1,...,u_i) and J_i := (v_1,...,v_i), with I_0 = J_0 = (0). Because phi is an algebra automorphism, phi(I_i) = J_i for every i. Hence phi induces an isomorphism of quotient rings bar_phi_i : A / I_i -> A / J_i, given by a + I_i |-> phi(a) + J_i; its inverse is induced by phi^{-1}. Now let u_i have degree d. Since phi is a graded automorphism, it preserves each graded piece, so phi(u_i) also lies in the degree-d piece. Therefore deg(phi(u_i)) = d = deg(u_i) for every i. It remains to prove preservation of regular sequences. Use the standard ring-theoretic definition: a sequence x_1,...,x_n is regular if for each i >= 1, the class of x_i is a non-zero-divisor in A / (x_1,...,x_{i-1}); if one also adopts the common extra condition that the final quotient A / (x_1,...,x_n) be nonzero, that condition is also preserved here because the final quotients are isomorphic. Assume first that u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence. Fix i with 1 <= i <= n. Suppose that in A / J_{i-1} one has (v_i + J_{i-1})(a + J_{i-1}) = 0. Then v_i a is in J_{i-1} = phi(I_{i-1}). Applying phi^{-1}, we get u_i phi^{-1}(a) in I_{i-1}. Equivalently, in A / I_{i-1} we have (u_i + I_{i-1})(phi^{-1}(a) + I_{i-1}) = 0. Since u_i + I_{i-1} is a non-zero-divisor in A / I_{i-1}, it follows that phi^{-1}(a) + I_{i-1} = 0, so phi^{-1}(a) is in I_{i-1}. Applying phi, we obtain a in J_{i-1}. Thus v_i + J_{i-1} is a non-zero-divisor in A / J_{i-1}. Since this holds for every i, the sequence v_1,...,v_n is regular. If one includes the additional condition A / I_n != 0 in the definition, it is preserved as well because bar_phi_n is an isomorphism A / I_n ~= A / J_n. Conversely, if v_1,...,v_n is regular, the same argument applied to the automorphism phi^{-1} shows that u_1,...,u_n is regular. Therefore u_1,...,u_n is a regular sequence if and only if phi(u_1),...,phi(u_n) is a regular sequence. Together with the degree argument above, this proves the lemma.

5. lem_20260329132438_1d671bdc: Let A be a commutative ring, and let u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_n be a regular sequence in A. Then the images of v_1,...,v_n in the quotient ring A/(u_1,...,u_m) form a regular sequence. If A is graded and all u_i and v_j are homogeneous, then the quotient images are homogeneous and keep the same degrees.
Let I = (u_1,...,u_m) and B = A/I, and for each j let w_j be the image of v_j in B. For each integer t with 0 <= t <= n, set J_t = (u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_t) in A, with J_0 = I. Because the concatenated sequence u_1,...,u_m,v_1,...,v_n is regular in A, two facts hold: each J_t is a proper ideal of A, and for each j with 1 <= j <= n, the element v_j is a nonzerodivisor on A/J_{j-1}.

First we prove the proper-ideal condition in B. Fix t with 0 <= t <= n. Suppose that the ideal (w_1,...,w_t) is all of B. Then there are elements b_1,...,b_t in B such that 1 = sum b_i w_i in B; when t = 0 this just means 1 = 0 in B. Choose lifts a_i in A of the elements b_i. Then 1 - sum a_i v_i lies in I, so 1 lies in I + (v_1,...,v_t) = J_t. This contradicts the fact that J_t is proper. Hence (w_1,...,w_t) is a proper ideal of B for every t. In particular, taking t = 0 shows that B is not the zero ring.

Next we prove the nonzerodivisor condition. Fix j with 1 <= j <= n. Let x be an element of A whose class in B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is annihilated by w_j. By definition of the quotient, this means that v_j x lies in I + (v_1,...,v_{j-1}) = J_{j-1}. Since v_j is a nonzerodivisor on A/J_{j-1}, it follows that x lies in J_{j-1}. But then the class of x in B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is zero. Therefore multiplication by w_j on B/(w_1,...,w_{j-1}) is injective, so w_j is a nonzerodivisor there.

Thus every initial ideal (w_1,...,w_t) is proper in B, and each w_j is a nonzerodivisor modulo the preceding ones. Hence w_1,...,w_n is a regular sequence in B = A/(u_1,...,u_m).

Now assume A is graded and all u_i and v_j are homogeneous. Then I = (u_1,...,u_m) is a homogeneous ideal, so B = A/I inherits the quotient grading, and the quotient map A -> B preserves degrees. Therefore the image w_j of a homogeneous element v_j of degree d lies in the degree-d part of B. Since w_j is nonzero by the regularity already proved, this means that w_j is homogeneous of degree d, so it has the same degree as v_j. This proves the graded statement as well.

6. lem_20260329132447_75e7cd4d: Let a and b be integers with 0 <= a <= b. Put I := {a+1,...,b}, let S := Q[y_1,...,y_b] with weighted grading deg(y_i)=i, and let R := Q[x_s : s in I] with weighted grading deg(x_s)=s. Then the quotient S/(y_1,...,y_a) is canonically isomorphic to R as a graded Q-algebra, via the map sending the class of y_s to x_s for each s in I. Under this graded isomorphism, homogeneous regular sequences correspond and weighted degrees are preserved. When a=b, both rings are Q.

statement_nl: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}, and let R := Q[x_s : s in I] be the polynomial ring graded by deg(x_s) = s for each s in I. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. Assume M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Then there exists a family (f_s)_{s in I} of homogeneous polynomials in R such that deg(f_s) = r+s for every s in I, and the ordered list of these polynomials in increasing order of s is a regular sequence in R. If I is empty, this means the empty family.
